scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Gay Gordons emerged as a traditional Scottish country dance associated with military march tunes.
The dance is closely tied to the composition by James Scott Skinner, originally known as 'The Gordon Highlanders' March', which was first printed in the collection 'Monikie Series no 3' around 1890.
It grew into a staple of modern ceilidh dancing and was famously recorded by Scottish musician Jimmy Shand in 1942.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Gay Gordons functions primarily as an accessible, social dance designed for community gathering and participation.
Its simple progressive structure permits dancers to switch partners dynamically, reinforcing social cohesion across all experience levels during ceilidhs and folk events.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by couples positioned around a room facing anti-clockwise in a large circle formation, with the lady situated on the gentleman's right side.
Danced to music in 2/4 or 4/4 march time, the movement sequence relies on precise timing across a multi-bar structure.
For Scottish country dancers, the hand hold during the first eight bars is the classic allemande hold.
Watch for Allemande hold march, Progressive shift.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the Gay Gordons is set in 2/4 or 4/4 march meter, delivered at a light and brisk marching tempo suitable for social dancing.
Primary musical examples include 'Scotland the Brave' and James Scott Skinner's tune 'The Gay Gordons'.
Listen for the Accordion, Fiddle.
The pulse is 2/4 or 4/4.
A brisk Scottish march tune set in 2/4 or 4/4 meter. The music features driving accordion or fiddle melodies structured around repeating phrasing ideal for circle walking and turning.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: As a popular Scottish social and country dance, the Gay Gordons requires no specialized ritual costume, though formal ceilidhs often feature traditional Scottish attire such as kilts, sporrans, and tartans.
It is typically performed in community halls, dance studios, and social ceilidhs where a large circular space allows couples to travel anti-clockwise around the perimeter of the room.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures associated with the dance include Scottish composer and fiddler James Scott Skinner, who published its iconic tune around 1890, and bandleader Jimmy Shand, who popularized the music with his 1942 recording.
The Royal Scottish Country Dancing Society serves as a major archival and educational authority for the dance.

While the basic pattern remains consistent across Scotland and international Scottish country dance groups, variations exist between standard social ceilidh practice and strict Scottish country dance standards.
The Gay Gordons belongs to the broader tradition of Scottish country dancing.
